question:
Patient note:
A 42-year-old woman was brought to the day-surgery suite this morning for an arthroscopic-assisted elevation and screw fixation of a depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture that she incurred sixteen days ago when she fell from a stepladder while painting her living-room ceiling; plain radiographs in the emergency department at that time demonstrated an isolated Schatzker II split-depression pattern without associated ligamentous injury, and she was discharged with a hinged knee brace locked in extension, strict non-weight-bearing instructions, and oral analgesia while operative scheduling was arranged. Since the incident she has spent most of each day reclining in bed or on a sofa with the right leg elevated, ambulating only the few steps necessary for toileting with a pair of axillary crutches, and she estimates fewer than two hundred cumulative steps daily over the past two weeks. She reports adequate pain control with scheduled acetaminophen and as-needed oxycodone but acknowledges stiffness from prolonged immobility. She has had no fevers, chills, night sweats, wound drainage, dysuria, cough, or other infectious symptoms and did not receive intravenous antibiotics at any point. She denies paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, exertional chest discomfort, palpitations, or lower-extremity edema. Respiratory review is unremarkable for chronic cough or wheeze, and she has never been hospitalized for lung disease. She recalls no prior episodes of blood clots in her legs or lungs, has never taken long-term anticoagulants, and has not noticed unilateral calf soreness, fullness, or redness during the current convalescence. Of note, her mother developed a leg clot during the postpartum period, and a paternal aunt suffered a pulmonary embolus after hip replacement, but no formal genetic testing for inherited thrombophilia has been performed in relatives. She underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy five years ago without complication and has not had any other operations, endoscopic procedures, plaster casts, major trauma, or hospital admissions within the past year. Her medical history is otherwise notable only for seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with over-the-counter loratadine; she has never been told she has heart failure, coronary disease, stroke, inflammatory bowel pathology, malignancy, connective-tissue disorder, or an autoimmune condition associated with abnormal clotting tests. She denies exposure to unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin outside routine peri-parturient prophylaxis nine years ago and has never experienced an unexpected drop in platelet count. Current medications include acetaminophen 1 g every six hours, oxycodone 5 mg up to three times daily, loratadine 10 mg each morning, and a daily multivitamin; she takes no estrogen-containing contraceptives, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoietin, or corticosteroids. She does not smoke, drinks a glass of wine on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Physical examination reveals an alert, seated woman in no apparent distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Body mass index is 24 kg/m². Cardiovascular exam shows normal jugular venous contour, crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with good air movement. Abdomen is soft, nontender, and without organomegaly. The right lower limb is splinted in a black hinged brace; the overlying skin is clean and intact, with no erythema, warmth, or fluctuance, and pedal pulses are easily palpable. Calf circumferences measure 36 cm bilaterally, and there is no pitting edema or tenderness along the course of the deep veins. The contralateral leg appears normal without varicosities or swelling. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact light-touch sensation of the distal right foot and full motor strength of the left side; assessment of right knee motion is deferred secondary to fracture stability. No central venous lines, ports, or peripherally inserted catheters are present, and peripheral access today was obtained with a single 20-gauge cannula. Laboratory studies drawn yesterday show hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 265 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.3 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, AST 19 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, fasting glucose 96 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an INR of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. Baseline electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm without ischemic or conduction abnormalities, and a pre-operative chest radiograph obtained for surgical clearance last week was unremarkable. The airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II view with normal neck extension, and anesthesia anticipates uncomplicated endotracheal intubation for the procedure. She has been nil per os since midnight, voided spontaneously an hour ago, and is positioned comfortably on the stretcher awaiting transfer to the operating theatre, where sequential compression sleeves will be applied before induction.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score sums weighted perioperative risk factors. The applicable factors are:
• Age 42 (41–60 years): +1.
• Planned arthroscopic knee surgery: +2; count the procedure once.
• Tibial plateau fracture 16 days ago (leg fracture within one month): +5.
• Family history of VTE: +3, counted once despite two affected relatives.
• Mobility is the scoring ambiguity. Using the 1-point bed-rest category gives 1 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 12. However, she was non-weight-bearing and up only for toileting for over two weeks, which more directly supports the 2-point confinement ≥72 hours category and would give 13 instead. The hinged brace is not a separate plaster cast.
BMI 24, no personal VTE, no known thrombophilia, and no estrogen exposure add 0. The total using the 1-point bed-rest interpretation is 12.
Final answer: 12
